title: Information Theory, Encoding & Serialization
summary: How you turn meaning into bits — and back — decides your bandwidth bill, your latency, and whether last year's data still parses after today's deploy.

blocks.markdown:
Information is surprise, and surprise is measured in bits.

- **Entropy** is a source's average surprise per symbol — the hard floor no lossless compressor can beat.
- Compression just spends **few bits on common things, more on rare ones**.
- Four layers stack: **encoding** (chars→bytes), **serialization** (objects→bytes), **compression** (shrink bytes), **hashing** (bytes→fingerprint).
- Get them confused and you ship corrupt text or break old data.

blocks.subTitle: Four layers, not one
blocks.markdown:
Each layer does one job; they compose top to bottom.

| Layer | Example |
|---|---|
| Encoding | UTF-8 |
| Serialization | JSON, Protobuf |
| Compression | gzip, zstd |
| Hashing | CRC32, SHA-256 |

One HTTP request can be UTF-8 text, JSON-serialized, gzip-compressed, and hash-protected — all at once.

blocks.subTitle: Entropy: the bit floor
blocks.markdown:
A rare symbol carries more information than a predictable one.

- Information content of a symbol with probability *p* is **log₂(1/p)** bits — rarer means more bits.
- **Entropy** is the average: `H = Σ p·log₂(1/p)`.
- A fair coin has **H = 1 bit**; a coin landing heads 999/1000 has H ≈ 0.011 bits — almost nothing to learn.
- No lossless coder can average below H. Everything else is engineering toward that floor.

blocks.subTitle: UTF-8 character encoding
blocks.markdown:
Unicode numbers every character; UTF-8 stores those numbers as 1–4 bytes.

![How a UTF-8 code point maps to bytes](assets/c12-information-theory-encoding/utf8-codepoint-to-bytes.svg)

- ASCII fits in **1 byte** (`0xxxxxxx`), so any ASCII file is already valid UTF-8.
- The **lead byte** announces the length; every **continuation byte** starts with `10`.
- That makes UTF-8 **self-synchronizing**: from any byte you find a character boundary, and one bad byte damages one character, not the whole stream.

assets.alt: How a UTF-8 code point maps to bytes

blocks.subTitle: Varints: small numbers, few bytes
blocks.markdown:
Most integers in real data are small, so don't pay 4 or 8 bytes for them.

- A **varint** uses the low **7 bits** of each byte for data and the top bit as a **continuation flag** (`1` = more follow, `0` = last).
- So 1 fits in one byte, 300 in two; only genuinely large numbers cost more.
- Signed values get **zigzag** encoded first (0→0, -1→1, 1→2, -2→3) so small negatives stay small.
- This is why Protobuf field tags and small ints are tiny.

blocks.subTitle: JSON vs schema formats
blocks.markdown:
Serialization turns an object into bytes and back; the formats bet differently.

![Protobuf field tags versus equivalent JSON](assets/c12-information-theory-encoding/protobuf-vs-json.svg)

- **JSON** is self-describing text: every message re-ships `"field"` names and ASCII digits. Debuggable and universal, but bulky.
- **Protobuf** ships a varint **tag** instead of the name; the names live in a `.proto` **schema**. Typically **3–10× smaller** and faster.
- The schema is the price of admission — you can't read Protobuf without it.

assets.alt: Protobuf field tags versus equivalent JSON

blocks.subTitle: Schema evolution
blocks.markdown:
During a rolling deploy, old and new code must read each other's data.

- **Backward compatible** = new code reads old data. **Forward compatible** = old code reads new data.
- Protobuf gives both: **never reuse or renumber a tag**, add fields as **optional** with defaults, **reserve** removed tags.
- Old readers **skip unknown tags**; new readers see missing fields as defaults.
- JSON enforces nothing — "compatibility by convention" is what bites people.

blocks.subTitle: Compression: Huffman + LZ
blocks.markdown:
Two ideas power almost every general compressor.

![Huffman tree giving frequent symbols shorter codes](assets/c12-information-theory-encoding/huffman-tree.svg)

- **Huffman** attacks symbol frequency: frequent symbols get short, **prefix-free** codes, so the decoder needs no delimiters.
- **LZ77** attacks repetition: replace a repeat with "copy *length* bytes from *distance* back."
- **gzip** = LZ77 + Huffman. **zstd** = modern LZ + range coding + dictionaries. **snappy/lz4** skip entropy coding — fast, lower ratio.

assets.alt: Huffman tree giving frequent symbols shorter codes

blocks.subTitle: Pick a format
blocks.markdown:
Readability vs size, and self-describing vs schema-coupled.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Public API, debuggability | JSON |
| Hot internal RPC | Protobuf / Thrift |
| Big evolving analytics files | Avro / Parquet |

If a human or unknown third party reads it, prefer JSON. If only your own services read it at volume, prefer Protobuf.

blocks.subTitle: Pick a compressor
blocks.markdown:
Compression is a ratio-vs-speed dial; match it to your bottleneck.

- **Bandwidth-bound hot path** → snappy / lz4 / zstd-1: cheap CPU, smaller payloads.
- **Storage-bound, read-mostly** → high-level zstd / brotli / xz: best ratio, slow compress, fast decompress.
- **Integrity** → CRC32/CRC32C for accidental corruption, SHA-256 for tampering and content addressing — never swap them.
- Don't compress tiny or already-compressed data; you waste CPU and may grow it.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
These choices run the systems you use daily.

- **gRPC / Google** — Protobuf over HTTP/2; tag-based evolution lets thousands of services deploy independently ([b09-api-design](b09-api-design.md)).
- **Kafka + Avro + Schema Registry** — a small schema ID rides with each message; the registry *rejects* breaking schemas at publish ([b06-messaging-streaming](b06-messaging-streaming.md)).
- **Git / S3 / Docker** — SHA hashes as **content addresses**: identical content dedupes, tampering changes the name.

blocks.subTitle: Signals in production
blocks.markdown:
Encoding choices show up as measurable signals — watch them.

- **Payload size on the wire** — drops after JSON→Protobuf or zstd; an unexplained rise means double-encoding.
- **Serialize/deserialize p99** — parse time is real RPC latency at scale ([d07-performance-engineering](d07-performance-engineering.md)).
- **Mojibake / replacement-character rate** — a producer isn't using UTF-8 or is double-decoding.
- **Checksum failures** — any nonzero rate is real corruption; investigate hardware, don't retry blindly.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"A character is one byte."** UTF-8 chars are 1–4 bytes; slicing by byte count corrupts text.
- **Reusing a Protobuf tag.** Old data on the wire is reinterpreted as the new field — silent garbage. Reserve removed tags.
- **Changing a field's type under the same tag.** Wire type is what matters; add a new field instead.
- **"Compression always shrinks."** It can't shrink all inputs, and random or compressed data only grows.
- **"Base64 is compression or encryption."** Neither — it *grows* data ~33% with zero confidentiality.
